a60.speaker: Jacqueline Musiitwa, USAID Deputy Assistant Administrator, Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance
a60.speech: Announced $1 million in aid for people affected by flooding in Niger. Met with USAID staff in Niamey with whom she discussed "the Agency's priorities, as well as development and humanitarian partners." Announced that earlier in the month, the United States committed to providing $1 million to help people affected by the recent flooding in Niger.

a60.speaker: US Embassy in Niger (press statement)
a60.speech: Said the visit "underscores the commitment of the United States government to collaborate on shared objectives in Niger."

a152.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a152.speech: Has said the US government’s decision to halt funding for HIV treatment in developing nations is a wake-up call for self-independence: “My own personal opinion on the executive order, which has now been reviewed, is that the level of aid and grants that is available from the US government to support charitable activities in developing worlds like Nigeria is likely to go down. I believe that it’s a wake-up call for us to strategise and think the way we do things and ensure that we also are able to exert ourselves and create some level of independence within our system.”

a152.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a152.speech: Said the government would identify avenues to raise domestic and alternative funds; said a series of meetings have been convened and there is ongoing discussion with United Nations bodies, WHO, UNDP and others that work within the health space: “For example, our HIV programme, which is heavily supported by the US government. We’re looking at crowdfunding to support that, in addition to the government making more funding available.”

a152.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a152.speech: Expressed optimism that the US government would continue to play its role in the global community: “I must say that the world is a global village and what happens in one country easily affects the other country. America cannot operate in isolation, just like Nigeria cannot operate in isolation, or any other country of the world, for that matter” ; “So, I believe that reason will prevail and the American government will continue to play the role it ought to play within the global community.”

a152.speaker: News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
a152.speech: Reports that President Donald Trump recently signed an executive order for an immediate 90-day funding halt for all foreign aid, including support for PEPFAR.

a152.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a152.speech: On 29 January announced an “emergency humanitarian waiver” allowing PEPFAR to continue providing life-saving HIV medications to low-income countries.

a452.speaker: Hafou Toure, Co-Chair of the AWLN-PSC (African Women Leaders Network - Private Sector Chapter)
a452.speech: In her intervention, unveiled a roadmap built around three major axes: the visibility of women leaders, their skills development and their access to decision-making posts, as well as the commitment of the private sector through concrete and measurable actions. “African women are ready. They are competent, they are innovative. They are transforming our continent. Our mission is to support them all the way to the highest levels of decision-making,” she declared.

a452.speaker: Sefora Kodjo, President of AWLN Côte d’Ivoire
a452.speech: Expressed her hope of seeing this initiative mark a decisive turning point for African female leadership, hailing the collective commitment around this vision.

a452.speaker: Yacine Fal, representing the African Development Bank (AfDB)
a452.speech: Recalled that while women make up 65% of the African agricultural workforce, they remain far too little visible in governance bodies. “Promoting female leadership is not a simple moral cause, it is an economic and strategic imperative,” she affirmed, calling for this priority to be integrated into public and regional policies.

a452.speaker: Myss Belmonde Dogo, Ivorian Minister of National Cohesion
a452.speech: Stressed that the empowerment of women is a guarantee of peace, prosperity and of a future for Africa. “Let us build ecosystems where every woman can dream, create, lead and succeed,” she declared with conviction.

a452.speaker: Joyce Mends-Cole, Executive Director of the AWLN
a452.speech: Welcomed the Memorandum of Understanding signed between the AWLN and the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA), which promises to strengthen the impact of actions in favour of the economic empowerment of women.

a452.speaker: Danièle Sassou Nguesso, Co-Chair of AWLN Congo
a452.speech: Launched a call to action to structure durable mechanisms for supporting female entrepreneurship.

a575.speaker: Edouard Sehlin, Director General of the Agency for the Development of Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (ADPME)
a575.speech: Said the ADPME is tasked with informing, advising, supervising and directing micro, small and medium-sized enterprises towards existing support mechanisms, supporting their categorisation, helping them seize opportunities and supporting high-potential enterprises ; “It may involve capacity building, advice, diagnosis or networking, and facilitating access to financing” ; explained that in terms of financing the Agency plays a catalytic role in order to encourage financial actors to intervene in market segments, or categories of enterprises, in which they are not sufficiently present.

a575.speaker: Edouard Sehlin, Director General of the Agency for the Development of Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (ADPME)
a575.speech: “All the projects planned in the SME sector have been finalised and are starting up with all the partners. We will do more, because this makes it possible to have an impact and to have a critical mass of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises capable of contributing to the structural transformation of the economy and of ensuring Benin’s prosperity in the future…”

a575.speaker: Modeste Tihounte Kerekou, Minister of SMEs and Employment Promotion of Benin
a575.speech: Said the PAG 2016-2021 amounted to around 9,038 billion CFA francs, with the intention of generating 500,000 direct and indirect jobs ; “We were already at more than 600,000 direct and indirect jobs more than a year before the end of the term. The PAG 2021-2026 is 12,011 billion CFA francs and 1,300,000 jobs that the government intends to create in good understanding with the private sector. That is why a good part of the reforms completed in the first term have continued, and their effects are increasingly visible” ; he mentions in particular the facilitation of business creation as well as the legislative framework put in place through the investment code, the law on the promotion of SMEs, and the law on hiring procedures.

a575.speaker: Modeste Tihounte Kerekou, Minister of SMEs and Employment Promotion of Benin
a575.speech: “We have an organisation of the craft world that has been completely revamped so that it complies not only with the law, but also with the provisions of the community code of the WAEMU area”; he adds that, in place of the former structure, a chamber of trades has been established by law, endowed with a consular assembly made up of 80 members elected by their peers, coming from 164 trades in accordance with the WAEMU classification of craft trades, namely 40 trade bodies and eight branches of activity.

a575.speaker: Urbain Amegbedji, Director General of the National Employment Agency (ANPE) of Benin
a575.speech: “The government has placed at our disposal new tools that make it possible to promote employment with more effectiveness and efficiency, notably the Special Programme for Integration into Employment (PSIE), which has been effective since 2020 and which today reaches around 3,000 young people who work in enterprises and whose salaries and all charges are covered by the State” ; assures that through the PSIE there is support both for the enterprise and for the professional integration of young people, with much more effectiveness than in the past ; explains that another youth inclusion project makes it possible, in a short time, on average six months, to train and put to work a young person who can immediately obtain a contract and start working.

a575.speaker: Robert N’Dah Sinkeni, Director of Crafts
a575.speech: “The Chamber of Crafts and Trades has as its essential mission to represent the sector before the public authorities and any other body, to defend the interests of artisans, and to work for the promotion of the sector.”

a584.speaker: Project head, PROTECT project (OCPH/Caritas Guinea)
a584.speech: "the PROTECT project, launched in May 2023, aims to strengthen prevention, awareness-raising and victim protection actions against trafficking. The project covers the regions of Boké, N'Zérékoré and Kankan, encompassing 7 prefectures and 21 communes, with the ambition of raising awareness and promoting behaviour change within communities. To date, the project has raised awareness among more than 527,000 people, trained community relays and religious leaders, and supported the return to school of 52 at-risk children. These results demonstrate tangible progress, but challenges persist."

a584.speaker: Jean-Louis Maomy, project head and representative of the interim secretary general (OCPH/Caritas Guinea)
a584.speech: Stressed that "the PROTECT project has made it possible to reach a wide audience," while noting that challenges remain, particularly regarding psychological and social support for victims, data collection and expanding awareness-raising nationwide. He therefore insisted on the need for integrated solutions linking the fight against trafficking to key areas such as health, education and social cohesion. He also expressed his gratitude to the partners and urged all actors to continue their efforts to eradicate human trafficking in Guinea.

a584.speaker: Alexious Butler, USAID Country Director
a584.speech: In her speech, welcomed the progress achieved through the PROTECT project and reaffirmed USAID's commitment to supporting Guinea in this fight. She stressed the importance of close collaboration with local partners, including NGOs, religious leaders, civil society and the media, to strengthen prevention, protection and prosecution of traffickers.

a584.speaker: Father Francis Oularé, representative of the Archbishop
a584.speech: Insisted on the importance of the commitment of every individual and every organisation in this fight, calling for new financial and technical support to help Guinea in this effort.

a584.speaker: Sekou Fofana, senior adviser and representative of the Minister for the Promotion of Women, Children and Vulnerable Persons
a584.speech: Highlighted the reforms undertaken by the Guinean government to strengthen the fight against human trafficking, including the creation of an Office for the Protection of Gender, Children and Morals and the establishment of a central service for the protection of vulnerable persons. He stressed the need for a comprehensive action plan to coordinate the efforts of all actors involved, with the support of technical and financial partners.

a630.speaker: Herculano, 64, displaced farmer and carpenter from Quissanga, Cabo Delgado
a630.speech: “We fled because of the violence” ; “Everything I had, I lost it. People's homes were burned and they were tortured. We saw the insurgents running after children to recruit them. We feared for the lives of our children.” ; described the moment the family fled in February last year as an “episode of horror”.

a630.speaker: Herculano, 64, displaced farmer and carpenter from Quissanga, Cabo Delgado
a630.speech: On life in the Nanjua B relocation site: “It's difficult for me, because since I've been here I haven't managed to earn even a cent. We want peace and to live free.”

a630.speaker: Isabella, 50, Herculano's wife, displaced from Quissanga
a630.speech: “When we reached Pemba, our feet were swollen and we saw many unaccompanied children on the side of the roads”, saying she felt lucky to have made it out with her whole family.

a630.speaker: Displaced women in the settlements
a630.speech: Raise concerns about the lack of lighting in the settlements and the fact that they do not feel safe in the evenings.

a630.speaker: Gillian Triggs, UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Protection
a630.speech: “This is a true humanitarian tragedy. A disaster that brings all sorts of protection needs” ; “I spoke to a grandmother whose daughter was killed during the conflict and the father of the child was beheaded and the grandmother is now caring for that child. Another woman I met is caring for a stranger's child who is now orphaned. This is common here, where women are caring for each other's children, where the parents have been lost.”

a630.speaker: Raouf Mazou, UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Operations
a630.speech: “What is needed is additional resources. We, as UNHCR, are working with the government, with the other international organizations to provide support, to provide help. But resources are needed, a lot of resources are needed.”

a630.speaker: UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency
a630.speech: Reports that some 670,000 people have been forced from their homes in Mozambique's Cabo Delgado province in a crisis that has failed to hold the world's attention, that more than 2,000 people have been killed since the attacks began in 2017, accompanied by widespread reports of human rights abuses and disregard for international humanitarian law, and says it is working with the authorities to monitor and respond to the needs of displaced and host communities, leading the protection response and providing emergency humanitarian assistance.

a696.speaker: Unofficial reports
a696.speech: According to unofficial reports, around forty soldiers died and 37 were wounded in the attack on the Chadian army garrison at Barkram, with more than 140 dead.

a696.speaker: Government of Chad
a696.speech: The day after the attack, on 29 October, launched an appeal to the international community to strengthen support and assistance in the fight against terrorism ; is asking the international community to intensify its aid and support to fight terrorism in the region.

a696.speaker: Political analysts / experts (unnamed)
a696.speech: Say this becomes a good excuse for an American military return to Chad; that by stimulating the terrorist threat in the region the United States is itself creating a pretext for the return of its military contingent under the mask of counter-terrorism activity, a strategy explained by the exhaustion of all peaceful means of arranging negotiations for a return to Chad; estimate that by sending humanitarian missions to one country or another Washington achieves quite different objectives, favouring its own political interests; and estimate that not all the allocated funds will be used properly, but that part of the budget could easily be diverted to finance terrorist groups in the region, thereby obliging the countries concerned to resort to American military aid.

a696.speaker: Major General Kenneth Ekman, US Army (interview on Voice of America radio)
a696.speech: Affirmed, in an unrealistic manner, that following an initiative by Deby an agreement had been concluded on the return of a certain number of special forces.

a696.speaker: Government of Chad (Deby government)
a696.speech: Flatly refuted Mr Ekman's declaration, calling on the American government not to interfere in Chad's internal affairs and to respect the country's sovereignty.

a696.speaker: Media and social media reports
a696.speech: Since last May, information has appeared in the media and on social networks concerning USAID's complicity in supporting terrorist groups in the Lake Chad region, in particular Boko Haram - that acting through the USAID office located in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, Washington provided financial and logistical support to Boko Haram, enabling attacks on border territories.

a696.speaker: US government
a696.speech: On 29 October officially declared that USAID will receive 572 million dollars in additional humanitarian aid to save lives in the Lake Chad region.

a927.speaker: Partners For the North (PFN)
a927.speech: Has recommended the National Planning Commission (NPC) as a pivotal player in implementing mindset change enablers essential for the country's development.

a927.speaker: Vasco Madhlopa, CEO of Partners For the North (PFN)
a927.speech: Articulated the organisation's belief that a change in mindset is crucial for fostering an environment conducive to business growth and job creation: “It has been 60 years since we gained independence, yet many aspects of our country remain in disrepair. The issues we face are not merely infrastructural; they stem from our mindsets” ; “If our minds cannot envision progress, we will remain stagnant. We must stop viewing ourselves as dependents on foreign aid and instead embrace a mindset of innovation and self-sufficiency.”

a927.speaker: Vasco Madhlopa, CEO of Partners For the North (PFN)
a927.speech: Urged all Malawians to actively participate in this mindset change initiative: “We must cultivate a belief in our potential as a nation. If we can change our thinking, we can change our reality.”

a1029.speaker: Government of Liberia, through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a1029.speech: Says it does not take lightly the potential strict travel restrictions on Liberia by United States diplomats and security officials.

a1029.speaker: Sara Beysolow Nyanti, Liberian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a1029.speech: Termed the potential visa ban a complete surprise while urging Liberians to remain calm as the government engages the US State Department to ascertain the facts surrounding the matter; argued that since taking office she has worked with the U.S. government to address some of the requirements outlined in the potential visa ban through formal letters and meetings in Washington, D.C. ; "The information received in the news and social media was a surprise. When the information came out, we contacted the U.S. Embassy in Monrovia, and they said that they had no information in relation to this report" ; "This was also reported in the New York Times newspaper. We are not taking this lightly whether it's true or misleading."

a1029.speaker: U.S. Embassy in Monrovia
a1029.speech: Said that they had no information in relation to this report (as recounted by Minister Beysolow-Nyanti).

a1029.speaker: International reports (unnamed)
a1029.speech: According to international reports, U.S. diplomats and security officials have developed a plan to impose strict travel restrictions on citizens from 43 countries, including Liberia, categorizing them into red, orange and yellow lists; the report further indicated that the proposed restrictions stem from concerns over weak or corrupt governance and security challenges in the affected nations.

a1029.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a1029.speech: Signed an executive order upon taking office in January instructing officials to compile the lists within 60 days, and described the list as necessary to protect the US from potential security threats.

a1029.speaker: Liberian government officials (non-response)
a1029.speech: Have yet to comment on this development; The New Dawn searched official U.S. government sources but found no confirmation of the policy.

a1034.speaker: Mohamed A. Hayir (Maareeye), Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation of the Federal Government of Somalia
a1034.speech: sent a stern warning to the traders who import low-standard seeds, noting that the government will take legal action against them.

a1046.speaker: Health stakeholders (at the 11th Annual Tanzania Health Summit)
a1046.speech: Have called for increased collaboration between themselves and policymakers to improve the management and prevention of the rising rates of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), while also working to secure reliable funding for healthcare services.

a1046.speaker: Research (unnamed study cited)
a1046.speech: Shows that individuals living with HIV are at a higher risk of developing NCDs such as high blood pressure and diabetes, which puts them at even greater risk of mortality if they do not receive timely and appropriate treatment and care.

a1046.speaker: Dr Redempta Mbatia, Executive Director of Tanzania Health Promotion Support (THPS)
a1046.speech: "We are witnessing a rise in non-communicable diseases in people who are already living with communicable diseases like HIV and tuberculosis. NCDs, especially high blood pressure and diabetes, are expensive to treat." ; "It is the right time to unite our efforts and work towards preventing these diseases in patients already receiving treatment for communicable diseases, which also require significant donor funding."

a1046.speaker: Prof Kaushik Ramaiya, NCD specialist and Chairperson of the Tanzania Diabetes Association (TDA)
a1046.speech: Highlighted the severe impact of NCDs, such as strokes, diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, urging people to change their lifestyles, particularly their eating habits and exercise routines: "Most NCDs, which are responsible for the deaths of thousands of people, could be prevented through healthy eating and regular physical activity. We need to intensify awareness and education on how to prevent and manage these diseases in our communities to save lives."

a1046.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a1046.speech: According to the WHO, NCDs kill approximately 41 million people each year, which accounts for 74 per cent of all deaths globally; of these deaths, 77 per cent occur in low- and middle-income countries.

a1110.speaker: Mário Ngoenha, director of the Office of the National Authorizer of the Mozambican Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation
a1110.speech: "Mozambique reiterated its request for the EU to consider resuming direct support for the State Budget," said Mário Ngoenha when reading the joint statement following the partnership dialogue between the government and the European Union, held in Maputo.

a1110.speaker: European Union (joint statement)
a1110.speech: In the same joint statement, the EU highlights the "need for a favourable environment to increase trade and investment flows with Mozambique".

a1110.speaker: Mozambican Public Prosecutor's Office
a1110.speech: Presented figures estimating the hidden debts, discovered in 2016, at around US$2.7 billion (more than €2.3 billion).

a1110.speaker: World Bank
a1110.speech: According to the World Bank, Mozambique was at the time one of the ten fastest-growing economies in the world for two decades.

a1267.speaker: Boni Yayi, President of Benin
a1267.speech: Announced his pardon of Patrice Talon in a solemn declaration on the night of Wednesday 14 May from the Marina presidential palace, broadcast live by national television, ORTB. Boni Yayi says he has forgiven, and extends a hand to his adversary.

a1267.speaker: Boni Yayi, President of Benin
a1267.speech: Has always dismissed out of hand the claim that his constitutional revision project is aimed at keeping him in power beyond 2016. On many occasions he has reiterated his intention to leave power at the end of his second term in 2016, recalling in passing the commitment he made before Pope Benedict XVI in particular. The Beninese president also misses no opportunity to recall that he holds to his constitutional reform project like the apple of his eye.

a1267.speaker: Patrice Talon, Beninese businessman
a1267.speech: In an interview given to RFI on 29 October 2012, claimed to be the victim of relentless persecution by Boni Yayi for having refused to finance the constitutional reform project, whose ultimate aim, to paraphrase him, is to allow Boni Yayi to remain in power beyond 2016, the date of the end of his second term.

a1267.speaker: Government of Benin
a1267.speech: In early 2012 accused Patrice Talon of manipulating the country's cotton production statistics and of cheating in the acquisition of the PVI-NG contract, and proceedings were brought against the businessman for economic crime; in the Sodeco case, the government recently filed a complaint against the Talon camp.

a1332.speaker: Hillary Chindodo, Chief Executive Officer of Changamiri Coffee Company
a1332.speech: According to Chindodo, the initiative is more than just a competition. "Zimbabwe's coffee industry has a story worth sharing. The Barista Throwdown is not just about competition, it is a movement to celebrate the people, flavours, and innovations that make Zimbabwean coffee unique," he said.

a1332.speaker: Hillary Chindodo, Chief Executive Officer of Changamiri Coffee Company
a1332.speech: "We are creating an ecosystem where Zimbabwean coffee can compete on the world stage," Mr Chindodo emphasised. "This is the time for investors, coffee chains, and hospitality brands to take notice." ; "Coffee is not just a beverage it is a billion-dollar industry. Zimbabwe has the potential to be a major player in Africa's specialty coffee market," Mr Chindodo added.

a1350.speaker: US government
a1350.speech: Wants South Africa to take action on the Expropriation Act, alleged race-based laws, and its relationship with Iran.

a1350.speaker: Some GNU (Government of National Unity) partners
a1350.speech: Criticised the DA's visit, calling it a betrayal and accusing the party of bad faith.

a1350.speaker: Lincoln Sebola, Police Lieutenant Colonel
a1350.speech: Found Racquel "Kelly" Smith's behaviour concerning during the search for her missing daughter, Joshlin. Smith allegedly made the comments about her daughter making her famous, which raised red flags for Sebola. Sebola also noted Smith did not seem worried about her other two children during the search.

a1350.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a1350.speech: Expressed dissatisfaction with the state of Gauteng, particularly its infrastructure and service delivery, ahead of the province hosting the G20 Leaders Summit in November. Ramaphosa urged Gauteng's premier and officials to improve the province's infrastructure and overall appearance to make a good impression on international visitors attending the summit. The president emphasised the importance of showcasing South Africa's capabilities and pride during the summit, urging a collective effort to ensure a successful and impressive event.

a1350.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1350.speech: Claimed nobody has ever heard of Lesotho. Trump made the comment while criticising foreign aid spending, including funding for LGBTQI+ rights in Lesotho.

a1350.speaker: Lesotho's foreign minister
a1350.speech: Expressed disappointment at Trump's remarks but acknowledged the US' right to cut aid.

a1350.speaker: Agent and husband of Crystal-Donna Roberts
a1350.speech: Confirmed that Roberts died after a battle with stage four breast cancer.

a1379.speaker: Dikeledi Sekopamotse's grandmother
a1379.speech: Used to look at her and tell her she would be a teacher one day.

a1379.speaker: Dikeledi Sekopamotse, principal at Platinum Village Primary School and winner of the National Teaching Award for Excellence in Primary School Leadership
a1379.speech: Said the road to success was never easy because she had to find way to take the school to new heights. "The developments I have put my educators through make me a proud principal. When I look at challenges now, I always remind myself that I can't go back and that this is nothing and I will pass through this."

a1379.speaker: Dikeledi Sekopamotse, principal at Platinum Village Primary School
a1379.speech: On entering the teaching profession: "To tell you the truth, it was not what I wanted in matric, but when I went into it, I started to enjoy it." ; "I worked with very experienced teachers, and felt their way of teaching was not for me. I then registered at the University of Johannesburg, which was previously called RAU (Randse Afrikaanse Universiteit), where I did my mathematics and education higher diploma."

a1379.speaker: Dikeledi Sekopamotse, principal at Platinum Village Primary School
a1379.speech: On arriving at the new school and its lack of resources: "Before I arrived at the school, it had already been in operation from Grade R to Grade 4 with new teachers, but there was no management or a principal." ; "When I first came in in November, I thought it was a nice building with a sports field, but when I went inside, it wasn't what I expected." She added that the school lacked essential resources, such as tables and chairs, and that the 11 new teachers, fresh out of university, had no idea what to do when it came to classroom management ; "It was tough. I had to start with resources, and the department was very helpful in providing us with teaching and learning materials. When I went to Impala, they brought in tables and chairs for us and teaching continued as normal."

a1379.speaker: Dikeledi Sekopamotse, principal at Platinum Village Primary School
a1379.speech: On low enrolment in 2018: "At the time, we had two double-storey blocks but only occupied one. When I asked parents why they sent their children to other schools when there is one nearby, they responded that it was a new school and they knew nothing about it."

a1379.speaker: Dikeledi Sekopamotse, principal at Platinum Village Primary School
a1379.speech: Said her future plans would set Platinum Village Primary School apart from those in the rest in Rustenburg.

a1512.speaker: Salayea Magisterial Court
a1512.speech: Dismissed the case because the miners had a valid license, and advised the Ministry of Mines and Energy and the Forestry Development Authority (FDA) to settle the matter administratively.

a1512.speaker: Global Forest Watch, an online platform that monitors forests worldwide
a1512.speech: According to Global Forest Watch, from 2002 Liberia lost 347,000 hectares of primary forest, with 20,000 hectares in Lofa County last year alone.

a1512.speaker: Yassah Mulbah, chief officer of the Salayea Community Forest
a1512.speech: "What is happening in the community is bad because they are damaging the forest that we are fighting to protect for our children and the future generation" ; "We are not happy because they are still destroying our forests, cutting down trees, and spoiling rivers and creeks because of gold-digging business."

a1512.speaker: World Bank
a1512.speech: According to the World Bank, mining contributed $665.4 million to Liberia's GDP last year and was a primary driver of economic growth along with construction; continued growth of 5.3 percent is projected for 2024 and an average of 5.6 percent between 2024 and 2025, spurred by mining and structural reforms.

a1512.speaker: Locals of Korninga B Community Forest, Gbarpolu
a1512.speech: Sued Bea Mountain company for unauthorized entry into the community forest, accusing the company of cutting and destroying 2,800 logs while exploring for gold.

a1512.speaker: 16th Judicial Circuit Court in Bopolu
a1512.speech: Found the Turkish-owned company liable and ordered it to pay over US$1.3 million in special damages and an additional US$3 million in general damages.

a1512.speaker: Bondi Mandingo Authorized Community Forest, Gbarpolu
a1512.speech: Filed a $500,000 lawsuit against Harming Mining Group of Companies, accusing the company of cutting trees, digging large pits polluting water sources and establishing a camp protected by armed police.

a1512.speaker: Forestry campaigners
a1512.speech: Say the cases expose the lack of coordination between the Ministry of Mines and the FDA, corruption and other issues.

a1512.speaker: USAID (2018 report)
a1512.speech: A 2018 USAID report established that the Ministry of Mines weakened local forest management by authorizing mining in community forests without consulting local people and the FDA.

a1512.speaker: Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) (2021 report)
a1512.speech: A 2021 CENTAL report highlighted weak coordination between the government offices in awarding semi-industrial-scale and small-scale mining licenses; it found no redress mechanism for dissatisfied townspeople, except the courts, and that citizens' participation in mining was low.

a1512.speaker: Dayugar Johnson, lead campaigner at Civil Society Independent Forest Monitors
a1512.speech: "In some areas, the FDA and Ministry of Mines and Energy lack the resources or capacity to enforce rules effectively" ; "This leaves community forests and... protected areas vulnerable to unauthorized mining activities..." ; Johnson thinks corruption, high demands for minerals, limited awareness of the law and lack of alternative livelihood are a part of the problem.

a1512.speaker: Rexford Sartuh, then-Assistant Minister for Exploration, Ministry of Mines and Energy
a1512.speech: Disclosed in a 2020 interview that the Ministry of Mines did not recognize community forests: "They have their right to their land but when it comes to the issuance of mineral rights in Liberia, we don't consider them. They believe that we should ask them before we issue [licenses]. We should not."

a1512.speaker: Wilmot Paye, Minister of Mines and Energy
a1512.speech: In a WhatsApp chat with The DayLight, Paye suggested that the mining law was superior to forestry laws and regulations: "Your query should further focus on what the Minerals and Mining Law of 2000 says", Paye texted, and did not say anything else.

a1512.speaker: Drafters of a new mining law
a1512.speech: Are proposing full recognition of all forestry and land laws and regulations, according to a draft seen by The DayLight.

a1512.speaker: Mike Doryen, former FDA Managing Director
a1512.speech: Criticized the Solway deal in 2020: "We are disappointed in the way the Ministry of Mines and Energy handled things"; "We think it has the propensity of discouraging our donors from making any more investments in the conservation area of our country."

a1512.speaker: Yassah Mulbah, chief officer of the Salayea Community Forest
a1512.speech: Says the FDA pledges to support Salayea, and that she and others have decided to sue the miners at another court ; "The community is frustrated, and people want to protest, but we urge patience as we seek help to protect our forest" ; "We are not satisfied because the government authorized us to manage our forest and resources."

a1522.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Finance and Development Planning Minister
a1522.speech: Has outlined the progress made by the Boakai Administration in determining Liberia's eligibility for the second Compact of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC), valued at $500 million, citing the establishment and strengthening of an intra-governmental team focused on monitoring the MCC Scorecard to ensure Liberia meets the requirements.

a1522.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Finance and Development Planning Minister
a1522.speech: Informed the gathering that the Boakai Administration prioritizes transparency and accountability, highlighting ongoing efforts to hold individuals accused of corruption accountable, audit ministries, agencies, and commissions (MACs), and form an assets recovery team as key interventions made by the Liberian government ; Reiterated the Liberian government's dedication to accountability and improving the lives of its citizens, adding that the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission and the General Auditing Commission are actively collaborating with the Ministry of Justice to prosecute those indicted in various reports.

a1522.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Finance and Development Planning Minister
a1522.speech: Stressed the need to reinstitute the US-Liberia Political Dialogue to strengthen relations between the two countries, stating that the US-Liberia political dialogue is a structured framework for the bilateral friendship between Liberia and America.

a1522.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Finance and Development Planning Minister
a1522.speech: Highlighted Liberia's constructive engagement with major international partners, citing recent achievements such as the IMF's approval of a US$210 million Economic Compact Fund (ECF) program and the World Bank's US$60 million in direct budgetary support; he noted that these milestones reflect the government's commitment to meeting critical targets.

a1522.speaker: Daniel W. Barnes, Managing Director of the Department of Policy and Evaluation Selection Eligibility and Policy Performance at the MCC
a1522.speech: Expressed gratitude to the Liberian delegation for their proactive engagement; commended Liberia's efforts in combating corruption and reducing poverty and pledged technical support for the intra-governmental committee focused on the MCC Scorecard.

a1522.speaker: Amy Holman, Acting Assistant Secretary for the Economic Bureau, US State Department
a1522.speech: Thanked the Minister and his delegation for the visit, conveyed her impression of the level of work being done, and expressed her commitment to working with the team.

a1522.speaker: Alexia Latortue, Assistant Secretary of the US Treasury Department on Fiscal Affairs
a1522.speech: Expressed the Treasury's concern about the World Bank IDA replenishment and that Liberia is a good candidate for the pandemic resilience program; assured the delegation of the US Treasury's readiness to collaborate with the Government of Liberia on the reinstitution of the US-Liberia Political Dialogue, the support of the US CDC on the pandemic resilience program, and the preparedness to work with Liberia on her fiscal programs, policy on public-private partnerships (PPP), infrastructure investment, and capacity building.

a1530.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a1530.speech: Called, for the sixth consecutive time, for an end to the blockade against Cuba in his speech at UNGA79, saying that "economic sanctions on States also contribute to forced migration, and the prolonged embargo on the Caribbean Island is an example of this." He added that, "in his opinion, this embargo should give way to renewed good neighborliness and cooperative relations between the two countries."

a1530.speaker: Gambian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (statement, July)
a1530.speech: Unequivocally reaffirmed its solidarity with Cuba, particularly with regard to the need to lift the blockade and exclude it from Washington's list of states that allegedly sponsor terrorism.

a1530.speaker: Mamadou Tangara, Gambian Foreign Minister, and Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, Cuban Foreign Minister
a1530.speech: Described the current bilateral ties as excellent in a meeting they held at the UN headquarters.

a1541.speaker: A specialist well versed in American affairs (anonymous)
a1541.speech: Affirms that "A return of Trump would mean a reduction in American involvement in everything to do with multilateralism, such as the climate issue, and possibly a reduction in development aid."

a1541.speaker: Many analysts (unnamed)
a1541.speech: Announce that a return of Trump to power would bring a new springtime of dictatorships on the black continent, considering that "African authoritarian regimes will be able easily and openly to renew ties with Russia and China."

a1541.speaker: Donald Trump, former US President and Republican candidate
a1541.speech: During his first term showed little interest in African countries, which he weaned off American aid through the withdrawal of the USA from numerous funds or projects, and which he above all described as "shithole countries."

a1541.speaker: General Charles de Gaulle (quoted)
a1541.speech: "States have no friends, they only have interests."

a1614.speaker: Mohamed Malick Fall, UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Nigeria
a1614.speech: Stated that the needs are "driven by conflict, climate shocks, and economic instability", with the compounding effects of flooding, disease outbreaks, food insecurity and malnutrition deepening vulnerabilities.

a1614.speaker: Nentawe Goshwe Yilwatda, Federal Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction
a1614.speech: Highlighted the growing humanitarian needs in north-west and north-central Nigeria and called for combined humanitarian, development and peacebuilding efforts for that region as well. "This will enable us to get humanitarian efforts translated into durable solutions that can move people out of poverty and provide livelihoods to reach sustainable development," he said.

a1614.speaker: Nentawe Goshwe Yilwatda, Federal Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction
a1614.speech: Said that the restructured Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction was committed to timely, effective life-saving humanitarian responses and poverty reduction. "We will continue to coordinate interventions at all levels, ensuring they align with national humanitarian and poverty-reduction priorities," he said.

a1614.speaker: Babagana Zulum, Governor of Borno State; Ahmadu Umaru Fintiri, Governor of Adamawa State; and Mai Mala Buni, Governor of Yobe State
a1614.speech: In their remarks, reaffirmed their commitment to sustaining collaboration with the UN and partners to address pressing humanitarian needs and foster sustainable development.

a1614.speaker: 2025 Nigeria Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP)
a1614.speech: States that a total of just over US$910 million is required to respond to the humanitarian needs of 3.6 million people in need of life-saving assistance in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) states in north-east Nigeria in 2025, with a total of 7.8 million people considered to be in need of humanitarian assistance; given declining global funding, the plan aims at strengthening efficiency in the delivery of aid, including anticipatory action ahead of floods and disease outbreaks, increasing direct funding to local partners, scaling up multipurpose cash assistance and reducing transaction costs.

a1620.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia (on fiscal policy and macroeconomic reform)
a1620.speech: Warned of an ominous period filled with seismic shifts in macroeconomic policy management, with transgenerational impact: "Successive administrations will benefit from our fiscal policy orientations. I'll not go into the details now." ; forecasted a robust 7.9pc GDP growth for the year and acknowledged macroeconomic misalignments he argued were inherited from past administrations, vowing to address them through sweeping reforms and referring to the need for "pinching adjustments."

a1620.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia (on the pain of reform)
a1620.speech: Likened the necessary economic policy adjustments to the acute, albeit fleeting, pain of tooth extraction: "A dentist is usually at the receiving end of insults. Only to be welcomed once the source of pain dissipates."

a1620.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia (on drought and food insecurity)
a1620.speech: Claimed "no single individual died from starvation" due to the expanding drought: "Drought is a recurring guest in Ethiopian history. It should not be used for political purposes." ; emphasised his administration's efforts to address food insecurity, insisting on providing over half a million tonnes of food assistance to the Tigray Regional State and efforts to boost agricultural productivity through mechanisation.

a1620.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia (on conflict, external pressure and debt)
a1620.speech: Cited 'unspeakable' external pressure undermining the successful implementation of prior economic reforms, and responded to parliamentarians' concerns over the proliferation of conflict: "The coming epoch is ominous. It has become far too easy to acquire weapons." ; referred to a global contradiction in which few have become 'drunken with money' while many more languish in worsening poverty, and dismissed insinuations that Ethiopia could not repay its coupon bond payment last month, referring to the country's import bill of 7.5 billion dollars over the past six months: "Ethiopia is much larger than that."

a1620.speaker: National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE)
a1620.speech: Unveiled a strategic plan set to span three years, targeting fundamental weaknesses in monetary policy and exchange rate management, with a notable goal of revising the foreign exchange reserve management guideline by June 2024, alongside a shift towards a price-based monetary policy system that emphasises interest rates and open market operations.

a1620.speaker: Mamo Miheretu, Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
a1620.speech: In December, stressed the importance of discretion in public comments to avoid fueling speculation about foreign currency management policy; he also disclosed ongoing discussions with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to enhance foreign currency management through structural adjustments.

a1620.speaker: Yenehasab Taddesse, director of foreign exchange monitoring & reserve management at NBE
a1620.speech: "It's not yet been formed," he told Fortune, on the restitution of the foreign exchange investment committee.

a1620.speaker: Atlaw Alemu (PhD), economist
a1620.speech: Observed a de facto floating foreign currency market, a parallel market system where most commodities are imported at nearly double the official exchange rates: "They might as well try floating it. Everything else seems not to be working." ; he believes that a committed improvement in capital and labour productivity could enhance the balance of payments, proposing that temporary shocks might yield long-term benefits if managed correctly.

a1620.speaker: Bartema Fikadu, MP from the Ethiopian Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA)
a1620.speech: Expressed support for the wheat initiative as part of agricultural economic reform, but questioned whether efficient market chains existed for local consumption: "Factories should not be short on supply if the country exports" ; pinned his hopes for responding to economic imbalances on the government's ability to deal effectively with the political frustrations that have become breeding grounds for insurgencies: "Calibrated compromises on all sides, reforms wherever necessary."

a1620.speaker: Several parliamentarians
a1620.speech: Raised concerns over the proliferation of conflict and the breakdown of a shared narrative steering Ethiopia's political course as the country's neighbours become evermore vocal over their regional anxieties and interests.

a1620.speaker: Tewodros Mekonnen (PhD), observer
a1620.speech: Urges nuanced analysis, arguing that the country's economic fate cannot hinge on single policy changes but requires a comprehensive understanding of the intricate relations between various macroeconomic factors; argued that the real economy - investment, production, consumption patterns, and balance of payments - responds uniquely to forex regime policy changes depending on the particular conditions of its macroeconomics: "There are no 'A' or 'B' type of solutions."

a1690.speaker: The Beginnings Fund organisers (statement)
a1690.speech: Said in a statement that the fund set a deadline of 2030 to reach the $500-million target and has already reached $450 million in pledges.

a1690.speaker: Tala Al Ramahi, spokeswoman for the Mohamed bin Zayed Foundation for Humanity
a1690.speech: "It's a very critical time" ; "Philanthropy cannot fill the gaps that the aid cuts have left behind," she told AFP, but the Beginnings Fund will target "the products, people, and systems required to improve and scale maternal and neonatal health".

a1690.speaker: United Arab Emirates (UAE)
a1690.speech: Denies any military involvement in the conflicts despite evidence presented by the United Nations and many other agencies, after being accused of complicity in genocide by Sudan through its support for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and of violating a UN arms embargo to supply weapons to Libya's eastern military strongman Khalifa Haftar.

a1690.speaker: The Beginnings Fund organisers (statement)
a1690.speech: The statement said most deaths in sub-Saharan Africa occur within the first month of life, and the region accounts for 70 percent of global maternal deaths; 182,000 women and 1.2 million newborns die each year from preventable causes, along with 950,000 stillbirths.

a1730.speaker: Mohlomi Moleko, Lesotho Minister of Natural Resources and Acting Minister of Energy (termination letter)
a1730.speech: "I write to formally communicate the termination of your appointment as a member of the Board of the Lesotho Electricity and Water Authority (LEWA), with immediate effect" ; "This decision follows a pattern of conduct that has raised serious concerns about your ability to continue serving effectively and in the spirit of collective responsibility expected of all board members of such a critical institution." ; "On 24 July 2025, a day after the termination of the Chairperson of the LEWA Board, you made a public statement on Facebook which, while not explicitly naming anyone, appears to cast aspersions on the leadership of LEWA and the decisions taken in the interest of good governance and institutional accountability." ; "Given the context and timing of this post, it is difficult to view your remarks as anything other than an attempt to undermine a lawful decision of the appointing authority and to cast doubt on the integrity and competence of other Board members." ; "Such conduct is not compatible with the high standards of professionalism, unity, and mutual respect required of members serving in regulatory governance." ; "Serving on the LEWA Board is not only a position of privilege but one of collective accountability. While dissent and robust debate are encouraged within appropriate forums, public disparagement of board decisions or the credibility of fellow members — especially through innuendo — compromises the authority and reputation of the institution." ; "In light of this, and to preserve the stability and integrity of the LEWA Board, I have taken the decision to revoke your appointment."

a1730.speaker: Khotso Masheane, dismissed LEWA board member (Facebook post)
a1730.speech: "Both successful and failed organisations often have the same board structures, policies, and meeting routines. But outcomes vary drastically. Why? The difference is not in the systems, it's in the people. Specifically, it is the quality and courage of the board members." ; "Successful boards tend to have at least a few truth-tellers: those willing to raise uncomfortable issues, challenge groupthink, and ask hard questions, even when unpopular." ; "Boards of failed companies are often full of agreeable professionals who nod along just to keep the peace. They do not rock the boat, even when it is sinking. Ironically, it is not a lack of qualifications that causes boards to fail. Many were filled with highly educated, experienced members — on paper."

a1730.speaker: Khotso Masheane, dismissed LEWA board member
a1730.speech: Defended his Facebook activity in an interview, saying he frequently shares insights on corporate governance and that the post in question was not related to the chairperson's dismissal: "I consult on corporate governance and human resources management. I do pro bono teachings on Facebook to help improve organisational performance. I have been writing these posts long before Mr Makotoko was fired" ; claimed the decision to fire him was arbitrary and not based on due process: "The reasons mentioned in the letter are not concrete. To claim that it was triggered by the 24 July events is baseless. I even posted the day before. This is an overreach." ; "There are processes that should be followed when dismissing public office bearers. For instance, in the case of Pashu Mochetsane, who was dismissed in a similar fashion, the court ruled that public officers cannot simply be fired without due process or representation." ; "My performance is a collective one. I cannot be judged individually. I was not incompetent, even during our PAC appearance, I answered questions and defended some of our decisions. He never complained about my performance." ; asked whether he would challenge the dismissal, said "I have not given it much thought. I am currently preoccupied with other matters."

a1730.speaker: Mohlomi Moleko, Lesotho Minister of Natural Resources and Acting Minister of Energy (non-response)
a1730.speech: This publication sought comment from Mr Moleko, but his phone rang unanswered before it became unavailable.

a1748.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a1748.speech: Called the bombing of three nuclear facilities in Iran a "spectacular military success" and called on Iran to quickly bring peace or said the US would go after other targets with "speed" and "precision": "This cannot continue. There will be either peace or there will be tragedy for Iran, far greater than we have witnessed over the last eight days," in an address to the nation from the White House ; "Iran's nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated. Iran, the bully of the Middle East, must now make peace. If they do not, future attacks would be far greater and a lot easier." ; described the three targets as the "most difficult" and said that if peace does not "come quickly" the US will go after other sites: "Remember, there are many targets left. Tonight was the most difficult of them all by far, and perhaps the most lethal."

a1748.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States (post on Truth Social)
a1748.speech: Announced the strikes Saturday evening in a post on Truth Social after all US planes were out of Iranian air space.

a1748.speaker: CBS News, the BBC's US partner
a1748.speech: Reported that the US reached out to Iran "diplomatically" on Saturday to say the strikes are all it plans to do and that "regime change efforts are not planned".

a1748.speaker: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister
a1748.speech: Said the Trump administration gave him a heads up about the attack: "President Trump and I often say: 'Peace through strength.' First comes strength, then comes peace. And tonight, president Trump and the United States acted with a lot of strength."

a1748.speaker: Military officials (Israeli)
a1748.speech: Said Iran launched hundreds of rockets and drones at Israel in retaliation.

a1748.speaker: The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), a Washington-based human rights organisation
a1748.speech: Says 657 people have so far been killed in Iran, while Iran has retaliated with missile attacks on Israel, killing at least 24 people.

a1991.speaker: LGBTQ+ activists (Botswana)
a1991.speech: fear that queer individuals, already facing significant barriers to healthcare, are being left out of the resumed aid programmes; activists urge policymakers and healthcare providers to ensure that LGBTQ+ persons are not left behind, arguing that access to healthcare should be a fundamental right for all, regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation.

a1991.speaker: Research study “Risk Factors to Mental Health Challenges Among the LGBTI+ Community in Gaborone, Botswana”
a1991.speech: found that access to healthcare remains a significant challenge for LGBTQ+ persons due to discrimination and societal stigma.

a1991.speaker: Dumi Gatsha, Director of Success Capital
a1991.speech: expressed concern that many suspended services tailored for LGBTQ+ individuals have not been restored: “Religious and cultural beliefs make it difficult for us to access services,” emphasising that while US aid previously helped provide inclusive healthcare services, the current situation has left many queer individuals struggling.

a1991.speaker: Dumi Gatsha, Director of Success Capital
a1991.speech: said LGBTQ+ persons often experience discrimination at public health facilities where nurses and staff may judge them based on their gender identity or sexual orientation, discouraging them from seeking medical assistance including treatment for STIs; noted that the fear of discrimination has led to self-stigmatisation, particularly among those who identify as nonbinary: “Many queer persons may self-stigmatise and avoid seeking healthcare altogether because they feel unwelcome” ; “For example, a nonbinary individual may not feel comfortable discussing STI symptoms in an environment where healthcare workers struggle to understand their identity.”

a1991.speaker: Dumi Gatsha, Director of Success Capital
a1991.speech: noted on gender-based violence survivors: “For survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) or rape within the queer community, the situation is even worse” ; “They often feel unworthy of quality care, and after enduring long-term abuse, many choose not to report incidents due to fear of further discrimination.”

a1991.speaker: Research from the School of Nursing, Faculty of Health Science, North West University (South Africa)
a1991.speech: highlights that queer individuals often avoid counselling and mental health services due to stigma, leading to increased cases of depression and anxiety.

a1991.speaker: US Supreme Court (ruling)
a1991.speech: overturned President Donald Trump’s aid cuts, reinstating funding for humanitarian aid globally, which has led to the resumption of various services.

a2019.speaker: Davido, seven-year-old Mozambican child at Nyamithuthu Camp
a2019.speech: “I drew my family in a car. I miss my home, but I’m happy to be with friends here.”

a2019.speaker: Loyce, nine-year-old Mozambican child at Nyamithuthu Camp
a2019.speech: “I drew a girl with a suitcase because we had to leave everything behind. I hope we can go back someday.”

a2019.speaker: Estere Tsoka, Unicef Malawi Emergency Specialist
a2019.speech: Emphasized that these creative spaces foster healing, allowing children to process their trauma through play and expression ; “The stories of Davido and Loyce are not just tales of survival, but also of courage and creativity. As they continue to heal, their artwork serves as a powerful reminder that every child deserves a safe space to express themselves and dream of a better tomorrow.”

a2019.speaker: Estere Tsoka, Unicef Malawi Emergency Specialist
a2019.speech: “Interventions include the provision of water, sanitation and hygiene facilities, child protection center, nutrition screening items, recreational accessories and health supplies. We strive to ensure every child thrives.”

a2019.speaker: Dominic Mwandira, Nsanje district commissioner
a2019.speech: “We are grateful for the support rendered by Unicef and other partners. We are making a difference in the lives of these vulnerable children. Through the collaborative efforts, the camp stands as a testament to resilience, community, and the unwavering spirit of children.”

a2105.speaker: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Cooperation and Nigeriens Abroad (Niger) (communique)
a2105.speech: Published a communique sharply criticising the management of the 1.3 million euros of humanitarian aid by the European delegation, stressing that this aid was made available "without it having requested it".

a2105.speaker: Nigerien authorities
a2105.speech: Say the EU Ambassador proceeded "unilaterally" to allocate the grant to several NGOs, notably the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the Danish Refugee Council (DRC) and Cooperazione Internazionale (COOPI); they denounce a "contempt for the principles of transparency and good collaboration" and particularly criticise the "arbitrary" distribution of the funds by region.

a2105.speaker: State of Niger
a2105.speech: Announced the launch of an audit into the management of the funds mentioned and a formal request to the European Union to also carry out an audit in order to "know the real use and destination of the sums allocated to the NGOs concerned".

a2105.speaker: European Union
a2105.speech: Announced on Saturday 23 November the recall of its ambassador to Niger for consultations in Brussels; in its response the EU expresses "its profound disagreement with the allegations" and recalls that humanitarian aid is provided "in a neutral, impartial and independent manner" through United Nations agencies and international organisations; the EU maintains its willingness to support the Nigerien population while denouncing any "instrumentalisation of humanitarian aid for political ends".

a2240.speaker: Chikwe Ihekweazu, WHO Africa acting regional director
a2240.speech: Says that with strategic investment and governance, African nations can fund their health priorities effectively ; speaking during a press briefing in Kigali, Rwanda, ahead of the 2025 African Health International Agenda Conference, he said there is need to map funding gaps and work closely with African governments to find sustainable solutions for areas that were being sponsored by USAID ; "The focus must shift towards internally driven strategies while remaining open to strategic collaborations" ; said this entails African governments prioritising internal revenue generation for healthcare, reducing out-of-pocket costs, and expanding universal healthcare coverage.

a2240.speaker: Githinji Gitahi, Amref Health Africa Group chief executive officer
a2240.speech: Urged African leaders and global stakeholders to rethink health investments to build resilient and sustainable health systems, and said Africa's economic and population growth challenges are deeply linked to healthcare financing ; "Sub-Saharan Africa is facing an economic crisis, and the lack of fiscal space is a major issue" ; "Investing in health must be tied to population development, ensuring that every girl and woman have the right to make informed reproductive health choices" ; called for investment shifts towards primary healthcare, warning that disproportionate funding for tertiary care leaves millions without access to essential services.

a2240.speaker: Githinji Gitahi, Amref Health Africa Group chief executive officer
a2240.speech: Said Amref had significant programmes worth about US$28 million in Kenya, Malawi, Zambia and Ethiopia that were being sponsored by USAID, the core of which was around maternal and child health, and prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission ; "So, as we speak, we are working with the governments to ensure that no child is going to be exposed to HIV because we are not protected during the mother's pregnancy. That's a risk." ; "We had programmes on HIV prevention testing. For example, we had programmes on what you may call running care treatment centres for HIV, what we call the comprehensive care clinics that have stopped." ; said Amref had health workers across Zambia, Malawi, Ethiopia and Kenya, among other countries, that were actively involved in care and treatment for prevention of mother-to-child HIV and tuberculosis, care and prevention that are out of the health system though they are still trained.

a2240.speaker: Claudia Shilumani, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention director of external relations and strategic management
a2240.speech: Called for sustainable financing for African healthcare, and said leaders across the continent should look at the need to explore alternative funding models, including public-private partnerships, to ensure long-term sustainability of health programmes and the continued progress made in improving public health.

a2320.speaker: The Americans / US international partners
a2320.speech: had threatened to downgrade and declassify the port of Cotonou; now they applaud the new import verification reforms with both hands.

a2320.speaker: Millennium Challenge Account (MCC)
a2320.speech: had warned that it would withdraw if the port continued to be a cesspit; according to certain leaks, it is said to have given Benin Controle a clean bill of health.

a2381.speaker: Eswatini Bakers Association / Eswatini Bankers Association (as named in the article)
a2381.speech: Cited rising input costs: global wheat prices, energy costs and supply chain disruptions as forces ‘adversely affecting the sustainability of local bakeries’ ; the government-approved seven per cent bread price increase was made allegedly at the behest of the country’s Bakers Association, responding to the legitimate cries of the Eswatini Bakers Association and local bakeries citing rising input costs.

a2404.speaker: USAID State Accountability, Transparency and Effectiveness (State2State) Activity
a2404.speech: Has called for improved budgetary implementation and performance in the health, education, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene sectors in Adamawa State.

a2404.speaker: Suzanne Myada, Adamawa Team Lead, USAID State2State
a2404.speech: Made the call on Thursday in Abuja during the Quarterly Budget Performance Hearing for Adamawa State House of Assembly and Priority Health, Education, and WASH MDAs; explained that since 2020 State2State has been complementing the efforts of the State and Local Government Areas by supporting and sustaining the ongoing public financial management and other reforms and providing training, building skills and capacity of the stakeholders in the State.

a2404.speaker: Suzanne Myada, Adamawa Team Lead, USAID State2State
a2404.speech: Underscored the need to invest in the people through the provision of health care systems, education, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene sectors, adding that the people remain the greatest resource in the State; as the State2State Activity ends in 2025 in the State, she called on the members of the Adamawa State House of Assembly and key stakeholders to take ownership of the programme, align the State’s plans with local government areas, harmonise their activities to forestall duplication and focus on development results for mutual accountability.

a2408.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a2408.speech: Decided to suspend development aid for 90 days ; has also expressed his intention to withdraw the United States from the World Health Organisation (WHO).

a2408.speaker: Esther Jackson (not her real name), manager of a reproductive health education project in Dar es Salaam
a2408.speech: Speaking to Mwananchi about the fear of losing jobs because of Trump’s decision, said the move has left many workers in a state of uncertainty. “After those directives, we were told at the office that the projects we were implementing would stop for a while. For now we have been told we do not need to come to work until we are informed otherwise.” ; She said the situation has already caused anxiety among workers about their salary payments and the future of the projects, and that there is little hope of receiving this month’s salary and perhaps next month’s, but her main fear concerns the sustainability of the project. “Trump’s policies do not appear to give priority to our sector, so we are waiting anxiously to see how things will turn out.”

a2408.speaker: Employee of an organisation running family planning projects in Mwanza (anonymous, name withheld)
a2408.speech: Said that although they still go to the office, implementation of the projects has already stopped. “We are not going to the field (the project implementation areas) at present. Our activities are concentrated mainly in the villages, but for now we have suspended those activities.”

a2408.speaker: Lucas Malembo, Executive Director of Malembo Farm
a2408.speech: Speaking to Mwananchi, said Tanzania will face major challenges especially in agricultural research, which is largely funded by USAID. “A lot of money from USAID went into research. We still need to grow further in the agricultural sector through research, but now we are at risk of going backwards. Also, the international markets we had begun to reach may be affected as well.” ; According to him, many organisations depend on aid from the United States, especially for agricultural projects targeting women and young people. “Institutions such as SUA (Sokoine University of Agriculture) have been doing great work to improve agriculture in the country through this aid. Now is the time to learn to be more self-reliant.”

a2408.speaker: Dr Luka Mkonongwa, lecturer at the Dar es Salaam University College of Education (DUCE)
a2408.speech: Warned that Tanzania must learn to be self-reliant. “Let us cut unnecessary spending in government so that this money can support the education sector. If we depend on aid alone, we will stagger when the donor staggers.” ; Said this is the right time for Tanzania to reflect and put in place strategies for self-reliance, citing the example of Burkina Faso, which has withdrawn from dependence on foreign aid and loans.

a2408.speaker: Muhanyi Nkoronko, education stakeholder
a2408.speech: Said many projects could falter or stop altogether if an assessment is carried out and it is found that they are of no benefit to the United States. “Programmes that were ongoing may fail to be carried out and the biggest impact will be on the citizens of the areas concerned, who will increasingly lack services and jobs.” He added that the Government should come up with an emergency plan to ensure that services of great importance continue to be provided.

a2487.speaker: Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) of Malawi
a2487.speech: Has said it is monitoring the situation at the Department of Immigration and Citizenship Services, eight months after bureau officials seized 28 mobile phones and cash from officers following complaints of alleged corruption.

a2487.speaker: Egrita Ndala, ACB Principal Public Relations Officer
a2487.speech: Told The Daily Times that the bureau is still holding on to the mobile phones it confiscated, adding that mobile phones that were not connected to alleged corruption would be returned: "The investigation has been completed, but we are monitoring ongoing issues at the department. Our standard practice after completing an investigation is to return items not connected to the case."

a2487.speaker: Egrita Ndala, ACB Principal Public Relations Officer
a2487.speech: Revealed in the interview that no additional arrests had been made: "The bureau has not made any further arrests since those conducted last year."

a2487.speaker: Egrita Ndala, ACB Principal Public Relations Officer
a2487.speech: Confirmed that some suspects were taken to court and had entered pleas: "Some suspects are in court and entered pleas last week. The case is ongoing."

a2487.speaker: Hillary Chilomba, ACB acting Director General
a2487.speech: Told journalists during a visit to the department in July last year that the probe would continue: "We are continuing our investigations. We have new evidence that will lead to further arrests. More arrests are coming."

a2487.speaker: An immigration officer (anonymous)
a2487.speech: "It has been over eight months since they took the mobile phones and cash and I don't believe this is a professional way of conducting investigations."

a2487.speaker: Nicholas Mwisama, good governance expert with Transparency Initiative
a2487.speech: Said the ACB had taken "too long" to address the matter: "It has been eight months and for the bureau to simply say they are monitoring the situation is unfortunate. We should start questioning the relevance of the ACB as an anti-corruption institution. Since its inception, we have seen little progress in addressing corruption and people continue to struggle to access services."

a2487.speaker: Office of the President and Cabinet of Malawi (letter dated March 17 2025 signed by Secretary to the President and Cabinet Colleen Zamba)
a2487.speech: Says the appointment of Macloud Anamchuma Kalindang'oma as acting Director General will remain in force until the position is filled substantively: "It has pleased the government to appoint you as Director General of Immigration and Citizenship Services (Grade C) in the Department of Immigration and Citizenship Services under the Ministry of Homeland Security, with effect from the date you report for duties" ; it stated that Kalindang'oma is entitled to the full difference between his current salary and the minimum salary attached to Grade C, that "All other benefits applicable to your substantive grade will continue to apply," and that his acting appointment would cease once the government completes the process of appointing a substantive DG, in accordance with provisions of the Immigration Act (Cap. 15:03).

a2487.speaker: Ezekiel Ching'oma, Homeland Security Minister of Malawi
a2487.speech: Emphasised the need for Kalindang'oma's commitment and dedication to drive the department's transformation: "Malawians urgently need to put passport issues behind them. We have to gather ground, and we are moving forward on service delivery to the satisfaction of Malawians."

a2487.speaker: United States government
a2487.speech: Has urged Malawi to address issues related to passports and immigration.

a2498.speaker: Ricardo Missihoun, representative of USAID and head of the technical and financial partners of the health sector in Benin
a2498.speech: Underlined the importance of the workshop; according to him, achieving the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and soon the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) would be wishful thinking with a health system lacking a well-structured and interoperable framework; the SDTIC is therefore an essential step for the development of Benin's health system, he argued.

a2498.speaker: Dr Pascal Dossou Togbé, Minister of Health of Benin
a2498.speech: Indicated in closing the workshop that the plan to computerise the health sector in Benin was born of the government's desire to make Benin the digital hub of Africa and of the translation into concrete actions of the National Health Development Plan; he also recalled the importance of the SDTIC, whose drafting process was officially launched on 22 January; according to the minister, the validation of the master plan represents an important step in the process of rationally introducing ICT within the administration and business services of Benin's health system, to improve its management and contribute to improving the quality of services offered at various levels, at affordable costs and within very short timeframes, regardless of geographical and socio-economic situation.

a2498.speaker: Dr Pascal Dossou Togbé, Minister of Health of Benin
a2498.speech: Stressed the other challenges that remain to be met for the effective implementation of the master plan, inviting the steering committee and the technical committee to ensure the mobilisation of the resources needed to bring the SDTIC to fruition; he also thanked the World Bank for its technical and financial support to the project through the PRPSS.

a2944.speaker: Department of Disaster Management Affairs (DoDMA)
a2944.speech: Has revealed that while the country needs K209.4 billion (about US$119 million) to roll out the national hunger plan, only K61.2 billion has so far been secured from the government and development partners, leaving K148.2 billion still unfunded barely days before the relief programme is due to start on November 1.

a2944.speaker: Wilson Moleni, Commissioner for Disaster Management Affairs
a2944.speech: Speaking in Lilongwe, said the situation is dire but insisted that the response will still target every affected person, even in districts not officially declared disaster zones. "The total number of affected people is 4.2 million, and all of them will be assisted, whether they are in declared disaster districts or not," said Moleni.

a2944.speaker: Wilson Moleni, Commissioner for Disaster Management Affairs
a2944.speech: Said funding so far has come from the Government of Malawi, the World Bank, UK Government, USAID, Irish Aid, Germany, Norway, the Netherlands, Korea, China, and the World Food Programme (WFP) - but the resources fall far short of the enormous need.

a2944.speaker: Malawi Vulnerability Assessment Committee (MVAC)
a2944.speech: Recently warned that prolonged dry spells and erratic rainfall have devastated crop yields, leaving millions without enough food until the next harvest.

a2944.speaker: Leonard Chimwaza, agriculture policy expert
a2944.speech: Described the situation as "a painful deja vu" for a country that has spent decades battling cyclical hunger. "It's heartbreaking that year after year, Malawi finds itself in the same position - begging for billions to feed its people. The K148 billion gap is not just a number; it's the difference between life and death for millions of poor Malawians," Chimwaza said.

a2944.speaker: Officials (unnamed)
a2944.speech: Officials fear that without urgent donor injections, food assistance could collapse halfway through the lean season.

a2953.speaker: Ministry of Planning and Development Planning (Liberia)
a2953.speech: Insists that the macroeconomic indicators are assuring, all pointing upwards.

a2953.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP), Liberia (statement: “MFDP Achievements for 2024”)
a2953.speech: “At the end of the 2024 which is the fist year of the Boakai Administration, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP) is pleased to avail achievements it made in the period under review including the stabilization of the economy, lowering inflation, crafting of the National Development Plan, payment of civil servants in time for Fiscal Year 2024 and negotiation leading to the announcements of Liberia’s Second Millennium Challenge Cooperation Compact. The fiscal house also recorded in 2024 strong fiscal performance and the initiation of fiscal decentralization.”

a2953.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP), Liberia (statement: “MFDP Achievements for 2024”)
a2953.speech: Reported that in 2024 the MFDP focused on advancing Liberia's economy, achieving a growth rate of 5.1 percent supported by strong performances in mining, agriculture, fisheries and services; that the economy is projected to grow at 5.8 percent in 2025 and average 5.6 percent over the medium term; and that the government has begun implementing structural reforms in energy, trade, transportation and financial services.

a2953.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP), Liberia (statement: “MFDP Achievements for 2024”)
a2953.speech: Stated that the inflation rate was 10.1% in 2023 and is currently 7.7% on average, projected to decline further to 6.6 percent, and that GDP growth rose from 4.7% in 2023 to 5.1% in 2024 and is expected to rise to 5.8 in 2025: “These figures reflect transformational policy interventions being made by the Ministry of Finance & Development Planning to enhance economic growth and development.”

a2953.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP), Liberia (statement: “MFDP Achievements for 2024”)
a2953.speech: Stated that the MFDP led Liberia's successful accession to the IMF's Extended Credit Facility (ECF) program, that the IMF Board approved an ECF arrangement worth SDR 155 million (approximately US$210 million) with an immediate disbursement of SDR 4.3 million (about US$5.8 million), and that the 40-month financing package is designed to support the government's National Development Agenda (ARREST) and aims to address macroeconomic imbalances, strengthen debt sustainability and attract additional external financing from IFIs and development partners.

a2953.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP), Liberia (statement: “MFDP Achievements for 2024”)
